origin.fact: The wild form comes from Pahang and the Bukit Merah area of Perak in Peninsular Malaysia.
One hobbyist article also lists Trengganu and Johor as places where it occurs.
The aquarium fish are farm-bred, mainly by farms in Malaysia and Singapore. These farms supply most of the high-grade exports.
It was put in S. formosus by default because it was left out of the 2003 study that split the species. Some think it is close to S. aureus, but most researchers treat the group as one species.
Farms cross colour types with each other, so many crossbacks are no longer as pure as they once were.
Vietnamese articles say the variety comes from Malaysia and rank it among the most expensive arowanas.

looks.fact: When mature, metallic gold runs fully across the back. Unlike the red-tail golden, its fins are not reddish.
Hobbyists grade crossbacks by how fast the gold rims of the scales reach the 6th (top) scale row. A true crossback has that row all gold.
A deeper blue colour in the scale cores makes the fish worth more.
The gold shimmers and changes shade depending on the viewing angle.
Vietnamese keepers look for large, tight-fitting, shiny scales, two whiskers pointing upward and a long body that swims calmly.

lines.fact: Blue base and purple base: the scale cores are blue or purple. Some breeders use the two names for the same fish because the colour shifts with angle.
Gold base: gold reaches into the core of each scale. This type shows its crossback colour earlier and can become fully '24K' gold.
Green base and silver base: rarer types with green or silver scale cores.
Platinum white golden and royal golden blue are premium related types that sell well in Japan.
Lines are getting harder to tell apart because many fish mix traits of two or more base colours.

keeping.fact: Use soft, slightly acidic, well-filtered water.
The tank must be long rather than deep: about 600–1,000 L for an adult.
It jumps hard, so fit a heavy lid that fits tightly.
It is a carnivore. Feed insects, worms, prawns, krill and arowana sticks. Feed juveniles once or twice a day and adults every 1–2 days.
Keep it as a single display fish, because it can be aggressive to its own kind and eats small fish. Large bottom-dwellers or stingrays may be suitable tankmates.
Vietnamese keepers advise gentle lighting for Kim Long, and strong lighting for red (Huyết Long) types.

breeding.fact: Fish mature late, at about 3–4 years. Females lay only 30–100 large eggs, and the male broods eggs and larvae in his mouth.
Few eggs per spawn and scarce supply help explain its high price.
Vietnamese articles say crossbacks are hard to breed, and only a few fish in a batch turn out beautiful.

health.fact: Drop eye (the eye tilts downward) is linked to surface feeding, reflections on the tank sides and some genetic strains. It is hard to reverse. Prevent it by feeding below the surface and covering the tank sides.
In Vietnam, eye and lip defects in arowanas are blamed on poor tank lighting that keeps the fish stressed.

buying.fact: Legal captive-bred fish carry an implanted PIT microchip, with a CITES certificate and a birth certificate from the farm.
In Vietnam, imported fish come with a chip and a certificate showing their origin.
Buy from a reputable farm, and check that the gold reaches the top scale row or is on track to reach it.

controversy.fact: The wild species has been on CITES Appendix I since 1975. Only captive-bred fish at least two generations from the wild may be traded.
The US lists it under the Endangered Species Act, so keeping one needs a permit. Florida and New Mexico ban private ownership.
In Vietnam, some people give arowanas cosmetic surgery to fix drooping eyes or lips, under anaesthesia, for about 500,000–800,000 VND.
Hobbyist articles say farms cross colour types, so purity is reduced.
